description: Pinned prompt suite for native-vs-vLLM distributional comparisons (DECISIONS D39). Ids are the canonical inputs; text is provenance only.

tokenizer.file: tokenizer.json (released snapshot, preserved in the b69 window dir)
tokenizer.encode_options: add_special_tokens=False; ids are sent verbatim to vLLM and to the device run

prompts.text: A short Rust module that groups weights by block and applies the scale floor. It shows the borrow checker rejecting a mutable and immutable borrow of the same map and the fix: collect the names first, then take a mutable borrow in a second pass. The example also exercises iterator adapters, total ordering on floats, and a small error type that carries the offending key name so the caller can report which tensor vanished. The module ends with a unit test that builds two tiny blocks, applies the scale rule, and checks the decoded values against the expected f32 results within a tolerance. The test is deliberately written without a GPU so it runs in continuous integration on the host, which keeps the kernel-level tests separate from the arithmetic tests. This paragraph is provenance text only; the ids below are the canonical prompt.

The Kullback-Leibler divergence measures how much one probability distribution departs from another. For two distributions p and q on the same discrete support, the divergence is the sum over tokens of p times the logarithm of p over q. It is always non-negative, it is zero only when the two distributions agree on the support, and it is not symmetric, so the direction of the comparison has to be stated. Renormalising a truncated top-k list changes the divergence: the mass outside the list is redistributed inside it, so a comparison of truncated distributions should also report how much mass the truncation keeps. Jensen-Shannon divergence is the symmetric and bounded alternative, and the square root of it is a metric. These facts matter when two implementations agree on the ordering of the top tokens but differ in the tail. This paragraph is provenance text only.

Numerical analysis grew out of the practical need to compute with approximations. Before electronic computers, tables of logarithms and trigonometric functions were compiled by hand, and the errors in those tables were studied as carefully as the functions themselves. The invention of the stored-program computer moved the subject from hand tables to algorithms whose error could be analysed a priori. Wilkinson's work on rounding errors in matrix computations established that the order of operations could change an answer, and that a stable algorithm was one whose error grew slowly with the size of the problem. The floating-point standard that followed in the nineteen eighties made the representation of real numbers portable, and it turned questions about rounding into questions about specific bit patterns. Modern machine learning inherits all of this: a model trained in one arithmetic and served in another is not the same function, even when the difference at any single step is small. What saves the comparison is that the difference is measurable, and that a declared tolerance can separate a correct implementation from a wrong one without demanding that every bit agree. The lesson of the tables is still the lesson of the kernels: measure the error, state the bound, and check the bound before trusting the answer.

The GPU memory hierarchy shapes what a kernel can do. Registers are the fastest storage and hold the values a thread is working on right now. Shared memory is a small, explicitly managed scratchpad that a block of threads can use to share data and to stage tiles of a matrix before multiplying them. Its bandwidth is far higher than global memory, and its size is the reason tiling exists. Global memory, backed by high-bandwidth memory on the device, holds the tensors; it is large but slow enough that every kernel is designed to read each byte few times and to reuse what it reads through shared memory and registers. The L2 cache sits between shared memory and the device memory and captures reuse across blocks. Memory coalescing is the rule that makes global reads efficient: threads in a warp should touch consecutive addresses, so a single transaction serves the whole warp. When a quantised kernel reads weights, it decodes them in registers, scales them, and multiplies into an fp32 accumulator; the decode is cheap compared with the memory traffic, which is why weight-only quantisation helps. Attention adds a second layer: the key and value cache grows with the sequence, so paging it keeps the working set bounded, and chunked prefill keeps the batch within a memory budget. A serving engine that ignores these rules wastes bandwidth and stalls on memory rather than on arithmetic.

A mixed-language paragraph exercises the tokenizer across scripts and spacing rules. English prose sits beside a Chinese sentence that describes the same idea, so the same meaning is encoded twice with different byte lengths. Le meme paragraphe continue en francais, avec ses accents et ses espaces fines, pour verifier que la tokenisation ne depend pas d'un jeu de caracteres unique. Then a line of code follows: fn main() { println!("{:?}", vec![1u8, 2, 3]); } and a short JSON fragment {"n_tokens": 150, "domain": "multilingual"} closes the sample. The point is not the prose but the ids: each script produces a different distribution over the vocabulary, and a comparison harness that only ever sees English would miss a tokenizer or embedding bug that only appears on non-Latin input. This paragraph is provenance text only; the ids are the canonical prompt.

Design a JSON schema for a tool-call API. The request object has a model name, a list of messages, and a temperature between zero and one; each message has a role of system, user, or assistant, and a content field that is either a string or a list of typed parts. The response object repeats the model name, adds a unique id and a creation timestamp, and returns a list of choices, each with an index, a message, and a finish reason. Errors use the same envelope with an error object carrying a type, a message, and an optional parameter name. The schema forbids additional properties at the top level so that a typo in a field name fails fast instead of being silently ignored. Version the schema with a string field and reject unknown major versions; keep minor versions backward compatible so a client can parse a newer response by ignoring fields it does not know. This paragraph is provenance text only; the ids below are the canonical prompt.

Quantisation is a compromise between the memory a model needs and the arithmetic it performs. In weight-only quantisation the weights are stored in a narrow format and decoded as they are read, so the model keeps its activations in a wider format and the kernels spend their time on memory traffic rather than on tensor cores. Block quantisation divides a tensor into fixed groups, stores one scale per group, and normalises the values inside the group before rounding them to the narrow format. The scale itself is stored in a small format, often one with an exponent and no mantissa, so the scale is a power of two and the multiplication is exact. This is the arrangement the released checkpoint uses for its projection weights: groups of thirty-two values along the reduction dimension, one unsigned exponent byte per group, and a power-of-two scale computed from the group maximum with a floor to keep the division safe. Activations are quantised on the fly with the same group size and the same power-of-two rule, which means the effective precision of a linear layer depends on the largest magnitude in each thirty-two-value group. A group with one outlier loses precision for every other value in it; a group with a small maximum keeps more bits. The choice is not a defect to be repaired by a wider format, because the checkpoint was trained under that rule and the server that serves it applies the same rule. The interesting engineering question is therefore not how to avoid the rounding, but how faithfully a new implementation reproduces it, and how to measure the distance between two implementations that both claim to implement it. The measurement is distributional: compare the probabilities each implementation assigns to the same prefix, over the same token set, and state the tolerance before the run. A single token id is too coarse a signal, because two implementations can agree on the argmax while disagreeing on the distribution that produced it, and a generation loop can amplify either difference. The honest report gives the per-position deltas, the overlap of the top sets, and a divergence with its direction, and it derives the acceptance bounds from the declared tolerances rather than from a second run of the same code.
